If there is a single stripe, specify its position relative to the zip or pocket rather than relying on the order of colours in a phrase.
Preserve the image in its original orientation

A screenshot copied from a social feed may be mirrored, tightly cropped or filtered. Look for readable lettering or a closure to establish orientation. Save the uncropped reference alongside any annotated version. If the only visible part is the upper chest, do not assume the back uses the same colour arrangement. Distinguish the features you can see from those you are asking the seller to confirm. This is particularly important when a front and back use intentionally different panels.

Use a simple annotation only when it resolves a real ambiguity. For example, point to the narrow charcoal stripe to distinguish it from a black shoulder panel on another version. Avoid covering the exact boundary in the picture. Name files or notes by the option they illustrate, such as “wanted pale-body version” and “alternative dark-body version.” Sending two unlabeled images can make a careful explanation worse if the reader cannot tell whether both depict an acceptable choice or one is an example to avoid.
Deal with colour names and lighting separately

A seller may use cream, ivory, beige and light grey as separate options. A translation can collapse several labels into similar words. Preserve the seller's exact option alongside your visual description; do not replace it with a personal name for the shade. If the label says ivory and the studio photograph looks white on your screen, state that the ivory option is the one you selected and use the panel position as the deciding clue. Colour perception changes with lighting, surrounding colours and the display.

When exact shade is essential, decide what evidence would help before ordering. It may be possible to request another picture or seek an existing reference for the same option, but an image still cannot guarantee an exact physical match to an item you already own. Two photos taken under different lights are poor instruments for matching subtle undertones. If you need a perfect match for an existing outfit, acknowledge this remaining uncertainty while deciding whether to proceed or seek a seller with stronger colour evidence.
Write the note in a format that separates requirement and preference

The first sentence should specify the listing, original option and quantity. The second can state the visual identifier and any relevant size. A final sentence can state what to do if the option is unavailable. For instance, a buyer could request one medium jacket in the seller's labelled option B, identified by its pale body and black sleeves, and ask to be contacted before any substitution. This supplies a concrete check without asking the agent to guess which property is essential.

If you would accept a substitute, describe it as a separate decision. You might accept the same panel arrangement in another size only after reviewing its chart, or another colour only if the original model and price are unchanged. Simply writing “similar colour okay” could encompass a reversed design that defeats the purpose of the purchase. If you have not reviewed an alternative, ask for its listing and selected option first. Seeing an option and authorizing its purchase are distinct actions.
Confirm the note survives the purchase handoff

Check the final order summary after submitting the seller link to iTaoBuy. The developer describes the service as reading pasted links and purchasing on request. Verify whether the imported selection still shows the correct option rather than the listing default. Read the quantity and unit price again; some versions of a two-tone design may be sold as a complete set, while another option covers only a jacket. The note supports the selection, but its presence does not correct an accidentally different purchase line.

Save the confirmation with the original option and the short description. If a purchase agent asks for clarification, answer in the same terms instead of switching to another informal name for the colours. If the seller proposes a replacement, compare it region by region. Ask what changed in body colour, sleeve colour, stripe, material and included pieces. A replacement that looks close in a thumbnail may differ exactly where the original description was most important.
Check the actual warehouse unit against the note

When warehouse pictures are available, start with an overview of the whole product. For the jacket, verify the relationship between body and sleeves before debating subtle shade. Then inspect the label or seller code if it is visible and compare the selected size. If a feature is hidden, request the specific missing view rather than asking for a general quality check. A back view can answer a back-panel question that ten more close-ups of the front fabric cannot.

Finish by retaining the purchase reference, the final wording and the photograph of the received unit together. If the correct option arrives, the record tells you exactly which version to seek if you buy again. If the arrangement differs, you can show which region is wrong and which order line defined the expected version. That evidence gives an agent a practical basis for a seller inquiry. A well-written note earns its value twice: once when choosing the option, and again when checking what actually arrived.

Photographs of reversible items deserve an extra label. Describe which side is facing out in the image and whether the opposite side is part of your requested colour combination. A blue exterior with a cream lining is different from a jacket whose left and right outside panels are blue and cream. Use a reference showing the intended wearing position when that distinction affects your purchase.
